**Everything that must change before this draft is sent to customers.** The draft is `larkpay-comms/drafts/postmortem-2026-04-checkout-outage.md`; internal ground truth for the incident is `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`.

1. **The claim "No customer transactions were lost or affected" (draft line 10) is false and must be corrected.** The internal timeline records that 1,284 transactions failed during the window and required manual reprocessing, and 37 were unrecoverable and refunded (`larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`, lines 9–10). Telling affected customers — who by definition experienced these failures — that nothing was lost or affected is the most serious misstatement in the draft.

2. **The claim "LarkPay has maintained 99.99% uptime over the past year" (draft line 3) is false and must be corrected.** `larkpay-comms/metrics/uptime-2026.csv` shows the rolling 12-month uptime is 99.92% (line 15), and no individual month in the file reaches 99.99% — the best is 99.96%. Publishing a provably false uptime figure in a contractual context is a liability, not just an inaccuracy.

3. **The claim "Our monitoring detected the issue within minutes" (draft lines 6–7) is false and must be corrected.** The timeline shows checkout failures began at 14:03 and the first alert fired at 14:50 — a 47-minute detection gap (`larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`, lines 3–4). "Our team responded immediately" is also generous: the on-call acknowledged at 15:05, 15 minutes after the page (line 5).

4. **The claim "The affected component was isolated and traffic rerouted" (draft lines 7–8) is unsupported by the internal record and must be corrected or removed.** The timeline records the actual mitigation as a config rollback prepared at 15:05 and applied at 15:20 (`larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`, lines 5–6). There is no mention of isolation or traffic rerouting anywhere in the incident record; the repo's failover procedure (`larkpay-comms/runbooks/checkout-failover.md` — shift to standby region, drain queue, fail back after two clean hours) does not appear in the timeline at all. As written, this sentence describes a response that the evidence says did not happen.

5. **Blaming "the on-call engineer" (draft lines 12–13) must be removed.** `larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md` rule 1 is "Never assign blame to an individual." Additionally, the timeline never says who deployed the config change — it only records the on-call as the responder who acknowledged and prepared the rollback (`larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`, line 5) — so the attribution is not even supported by the internal record.

6. **Internal system and role names ("checkout autoscaler," "on-call engineer") must be removed** (draft lines 12–14). Style guide rule 2: "Never expose internal system or role names" (`larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md`).

7. **The draft must be restructured to lead with customer impact and remediation.** Style guide rule 3 (`larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md`) requires leading with impact and remediation; the draft instead opens with a reliability boast (lines 3–4) and buries the vague impact statement. Concretely, the draft omits the impact facts customers need, all of which exist in `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`: the incident window (14:03–15:41 on 2026-04-08, roughly 98 minutes — the draft never says when it ended or how long it lasted) and the transaction counts (1,284 failed, 37 refunded).

8. **Minimizing and unsupported language must go.** "Some checkout requests failed" (line 6) and "the vast majority of requests during the window were served normally" (lines 18–19) understate a 98-minute outage with 1,284 failed transactions, and nothing in the repository substantiates the "vast majority" figure — no request-volume data exists anywhere in `larkpay-comms`. This vague, self-protective framing conflicts with style guide rules 3 and 4 ("No hedging") in `larkpay-comms/docs/customer-comms-style-guide.md`. The same applies to the reputation-defense paragraph at lines 16–19 ("engineering culture treats reliability as the first feature… our track record reflects that commitment"), which the uptime data contradicts.

9. **The draft must disclose the SLA breach and the service credits owed.** `larkpay-comms/docs/sla-commitments.md` states the contractual monthly SLA is 99.9% and any month below it is a breach owing service credits scaled to the depth of the breach. April 2026 came in at 99.77% (`larkpay-comms/metrics/uptime-2026.csv`, line 7). A postmortem going to affected customers cannot omit that they are contractually owed credits. (Corroboration that the CSV and timeline describe the same event: 0.23% of April ≈ 99 minutes of downtime, matching the ~98-minute incident window.)

10. **The remediation section is too thin and misses the biggest failure.** The only commitment (line 21) is pre-deploy validation of config changes, which addresses the trigger but not the 47-minute detection gap — the most conspicuous failure in `larkpay-comms/incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md` (failures at 14:03, first page at 14:50). A credible customer postmortem needs a remediation item for monitoring/alerting coverage, and cannot honestly claim fast detection (see point 3) while proposing nothing to improve it.

Process note supporting all of the above: `larkpay-comms/adr/0002-incident-doc-flow.md` requires customer drafts to be "reviewed against the style guide before send." As written, the draft violates all four style-guide rules, contradicts the internal timeline on impact, detection, and mitigation, and misstates the uptime record. Git history (`git log --all` in `larkpay-comms`: single commit `967b182` on `main`, no other branches or stashes) confirms there is no later, corrected revision of this draft — this is the only version.

For completeness: the workspace contains two other repos, `meridian-docs/` (a separate internal payments API) and `sched-decisions/` (a clinic scheduling product). The top-level `README.md` calls them unrelated, and a workspace-wide grep for "LarkPay"/"OPS-412" confirms no cross-references — nothing in them bears on this draft, despite superficially payments/checkout-flavored filenames.

- **High confidence** in the SLA-breach omission as a factual matter (99.77% < 99.9% is arithmetic); whether the credits disclosure belongs in this document versus a separate billing communication is a judgment call, but for a note addressed to affected customers I consider omitting the breach entirely unacceptable.
- **Medium-high confidence** on "isolated and traffic rerouted" being false: my evidence is the timeline's silence (it records only a rollback) plus the unused failover runbook. I cannot fully rule out that a reroute happened and went unrecorded, but a customer-facing claim needs positive evidence, and none exists here.
- **Gaps:** the timeline has no request-volume data, so I can neither confirm nor refute "vast majority of requests served normally" — my finding is that it is unsupported, not that it is proven false. The timeline also doesn't identify who deployed the config change, its timezone, or the deploy time (only 14:03 failure onset), and the repo has a single commit, so there is no history showing how the draft evolved or who authored it. Finally, my initial `find` was truncated at 100 lines, which briefly hid `incidents/OPS-412-timeline.md`; `git ls-tree` caught it, and I verified every tracked file in `larkpay-comms` was read.
